study.title: Overview of evidence-based research on acupuncture for stroke treatment using magnetic resonance imaging technology
study.study_design: Systematic review and evidence mapping of neuroimaging studies on acupuncture for stroke treatment using MRI
study.population: Patients diagnosed with stroke; study subjects underwent two MRI scans before or after acupuncture or one MRI scan during acupuncture
study.disease_condition: Stroke (primarily ischemic stroke; also haemorrhagic stroke)
study.inclusion_criteria: (1) Study types: clinical studies on acupuncture for stroke, limited to journal articles. (2) Participants: diagnosed with stroke based on various diagnostic criteria; subjects underwent two MRI scans before or after acupuncture or one MRI scan during acupuncture. (3) Intervention types: experimental group received acupuncture therapy alone or in combination with other conventional therapies. (4) Type of control: control group evaluated effects of acupuncture, with participants receiving sham acupuncture (SA), placebo acupuncture, no treatment, drugs, Chinese medicine, rehabilitation therapy, or other therapies. (5) Types of outcome: at least one MRI technique was used, resulting in MRI outcome measures.
study.exclusion_criteria: (1) Animal experiments, reviews, case studies, experience reports, or protocols; (2) Duplicate studies or data; (3) Studies where contacting the author via email did not resolve missing data or yield the necessary information.

extraction_notes.note: This is a systematic review / evidence map, not a primary study. All extracted 'results' are aggregate summaries across 158 included studies. No individual patient-level data, coordinates, or statistics from primary studies are reported in the review text itself beyond narrative summaries.

No neuroimaging coordinate tables are reported in this review article. All neural results are narrative summaries of findings across multiple included studies. Individual study coordinates, statistical maps, and precise values are not available from this paper.
Sensory/interoceptive response data (deqi, pain, etc.) are not systematically extracted or tabulated in this review. Only general narrative statements about deqi effects are provided.
Expectancy, blinding success, and credibility measures are not systematically assessed or reported across included studies. The review only notes suboptimal sham acupuncture reporting quality.
Adverse events are not reported or tabulated in this review article.
Detailed MRI acquisition parameters (field strength, TR, TE, voxel size, smoothing, preprocessing software) are not reported at the review level as these vary across 158 included primary studies.
Arms defined in this extraction represent categories of comparison groups used across included studies, not arms of a single trial. Sample sizes per arm cannot be extracted from the review.

The review references specific included studies (e.g., Zhao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2013) with brief result descriptions but does not provide tabulated data from those studies. Extracted neural results represent narrative summaries only.
Detailed search strategies are provided in 'Supplementary file S1' which was not available for extraction. This may contain additional methodological details.

The review states that the overall methodological quality of the included studies was 'moderate to high' but does not provide specific quality assessment scores or tool details (e.g., RoB 2, GRADE) in the extracted text.
The n_total_analyzed_neuroimaging is set to 158 representing the 158 included studies (not individual participants). Total participant numbers across studies are not aggregated in the review text.
The review states sample sizes ranged from 5 to 200 per study, with 68.35% having 1-50 participants. Total participants pooled across all 158 studies is not reported.
The study classification as 'RCT: 97 (61.4%)' and 'Non-RCT: 61 (38.6%)' refers to distribution of included study types, not the design of this review itself.

The specific acupoints used across the included studies are not systematically tabulated in this review. The review refers to acupoints such as Yanglingquan (GB34), Waiguan (TE5), Baihui, Qiuxu in narrative descriptions of specific cited studies, but no comprehensive acupoint frequency table is provided.
